1324.title: The cost of mercy
1324.hook: Dorothy Day lived the works of mercy at a personal cost
1324.howItsDone: Catholics practice the corporal works of mercy through soup kitchens, prison and hospital visits, and houses of hospitality like those of the Catholic Worker movement, which Dorothy Day co-founded.

segments.voice: Yesterday, caritas: love that gives itself, organized into the Church's service of the poor. Your line was charity everywhere.

Soup on a stove in a New York kitchen. Coffee for whoever comes in off the street. Beds upstairs, not enough of them, and a woman who lives in the same house as the people she feeds, eats the same soup, and shares the same bathroom. Her name was Dorothy Day, and you met her on day nine hundred thirteen. With a friend, Peter Maurin, she started a newspaper called the Catholic Worker, and then houses of hospitality where people in need could simply stay. Yesterday's charity was organized and wide. Today, what it costs the one who gives.
screen: `SOUP, COFFEE, NOT ENOUGH BEDS.` → `DOROTHY DAY.` → `HOUSES OF HOSPITALITY.`

segments.voice: Her rulebook was Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus lists the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner, and says that whatever is done for them is done for him. "I was a stranger, and you took me in," in the Douay-Rheims. The Church gathers those deeds into the corporal works of mercy, and Day treated them less as good ideas and more as a daily schedule. Then the cost. Living with the poor meant noise, smells, theft, people who were sick or angry or drunk, and very little privacy. It meant being tired most of the time. She went to jail for her protests. Mercy, in her house, wasn't something you dropped off on your way somewhere nicer. So why doesn't the cost cancel it? The story is told that Day didn't want to be called a saint, because a saint is easy to admire and easy to dismiss. If she was special, nobody else had to do it. She wanted the works of mercy to look ordinary and within reach. Her cause for canonization has been opened anyway, and she is now called a Servant of God. Now the carry. Some mercy costs nothing, and it's still good. But Day's life suggests that when mercy starts to cost you, sleep, comfort, money, the good opinion of others, that's often when it stops being a gesture and starts being love. Not suffering for its own sake. The cost is what makes it a gift.

segments.voice: Let Matthew's list walk slowly past, hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick, prisoner, and notice which one tugs at you. Ask what a kindness there would really cost, an hour, a visit you've put off, a meal with someone hard to be around, and if there's reluctance, look at it honestly. If you pray, ask for the nerve to pay it.
The cost of mercy. Dorothy Day's lesson: the works of mercy lived at a price, and the price turns a gesture into a gift.
Your line: the cost is the point. Dorothy Day lived it under one roof with the people she fed. Until tomorrow.

1325.title: Social teaching at home
1325.hook: how we shop, work, vote and spend time, weighed in conscience
1325.howItsDone: Catholics form their consciences through prayer, scripture and Church teaching, and some use an examination of conscience that includes how they spend, work, vote and treat others; parishes and bishops' conferences publish guides for this.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cost of mercy: Dorothy Day, living under one roof with the people she fed. Your line was the cost is the point.

A receipt from the grocery store. A calendar with this week's hours on it. A ballot, or a reminder that one is coming. A phone with a screen-time report you'd rather not open. Not one of them looks like a papal letter. But this block of the path has walked through letters on wages, peace, migrants and the earth, and every one ends up here, in small choices on an ordinary day. Today the big teaching comes home, and meets a word the Church takes very seriously: conscience.
screen: `A RECEIPT, A CALENDAR, A BALLOT.` → `THE LETTERS COME HOME.` → `CONSCIENCE.`

segments.voice: You met conscience on day three hundred ten; here it goes to work. The Second Vatican Council calls it a person's most secret core and sanctuary, where they are alone with God, whose voice echoes in their depths. The Catechism adds that a conscience needs forming, by prayer, scripture, the Church's teaching and honest advice. It isn't just a feeling. It's where choices get weighed. Start with shopping. Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote that buying something is always a moral act, not only an economic one. A price tag hides a chain of hands: who grew it, who sewed it, who hauled it, what it did to the land. Conscience at the checkout means letting that chain be seen, at least sometimes. Then work and voting. Earlier this block taught that work has dignity, and that the Church offers principles, not a party platform. So Catholics can weigh the same teaching and still vote differently. The Church asks that the weighing be honest, with every principle on the scale, not just the convenient ones. Then time. A Sabbath, rest, a meal with the family, an hour for someone lonely: how time is spent says what matters. Jesus gives the small-and-great rule in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater." Social teaching is rarely lived at a summit. It's lived at a register, an inbox, a ballot box, a kitchen table, one ordinary choice at a time.

1326.title: Social teaching close
1326.hook: love of neighbor, built into how we live together
1326.howItsDone: Catholics live social teaching both in direct works of mercy and in longer commitments: volunteering on a schedule, giving regularly, joining parish justice groups, and taking part in public life with the Church's principles in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, social teaching at home: the big letters weighed in small choices. Your line was conscience at the checkout.

A bridge carries strangers across a river all day long, and hardly anyone crossing it thinks about it. Somebody did, once. Somebody calculated the load, the wind, the winter, so that people they'd never meet could get home safely. That's care that doesn't look like care. It looks like steel and paperwork. This block of the path began with a phrase, love, organized, and it ends today with a picture close to that bridge: love of neighbor, built into the way people live together.
screen: `A BRIDGE FULL OF STRANGERS.` → `CARE THAT LOOKS LIKE STEEL.` → `LOVE, BUILT IN.`

segments.voice: Start with the old command. Paul writes to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." One person carrying another's load. Catholic social teaching asks a second question: what if the load could be made lighter for everyone, before anyone has to carry it alone? Then two ways to love. Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote of the love of one neighbor, face to face, and also an institutional path of charity, where love works through law, economics and politics for the common good. He called that second path no less a form of love than the first. Pope Francis, for his part, speaks of political love, the love that builds a fairer society for people one will never meet. Then the block, added up. Every life. Everyone takes part. Rights and duties. The poor first. Work has dignity. One family. Our common home. Markets have limits. Nothing and no one thrown away. Each one is love of neighbor, set into something that outlasts a single good deed. Last, what it doesn't replace. Benedict was clear that no structure will ever make person-to-person love unnecessary. There will always be someone lonely, someone grieving, someone who needs a face, not a policy. So the Church asks for both: the hand on the shoulder, and the bridge. Love made structural isn't love made cold. It's love that keeps working after you've gone home.

1327.title: Four Marian dogmas
1327.hook: Mother of God, ever-virgin, Immaculate Conception, Assumption
1327.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate these teachings at feasts through the Church's year, including Mary, Mother of God, the Immaculate Conception and the Assumption, and the Hail Mary greets her as Mother of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday the social teaching block closed. Your line was love made structural.

An older woman in the hill country, expecting a child she never thought she'd have, hears someone at the door. It's Mary, her kinswoman, who has hurried there. And Elizabeth, in Luke's Gospel, cries out, in the Douay-Rheims: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" Long after, the Church would sit with words like these and ask what exactly they mean. A new block begins today: Mary, her feasts, her titles and her teaching. It starts with a word that sounds stiff and cold, and turns out to be neither: dogma.
screen: `A KNOCK IN THE HILL COUNTRY.` → `THE MOTHER OF MY LORD.` → `A NEW BLOCK: MARY.`

segments.voice: In the Catechism, a dogma is a truth the Church teaches as revealed by God, in a definitive way that asks for the assent of faith. It also gives a gentle picture: dogmas are lights along the path of faith, making it safe. Four concern Mary. One: Mother of God, which you met on day eighty. A council at Ephesus affirmed for Mary the Greek title Theotokos, God-bearer, because the child she carried is one person, truly God and truly man. The title is first about who Jesus is. Two: ever virgin. Mary stayed a virgin before, during and after the birth of Jesus; tomorrow takes that one slowly. Three: the Immaculate Conception. Pope Pius the Ninth taught that Mary, from the first moment of her own life, was kept free from original sin, by the grace of God and in view of what her son would do. It's about her conception, not Jesus' birth, an easy mix-up. Four: the Assumption. Pope Pius the Twelfth taught that at the end of her earthly life Mary was taken up, body and soul, into heavenly glory. Why hold them together? Each one points back to Christ: who he is, how he came, what his saving work does, and where it leads. The Church sees in Mary what grace can do in one human life. And who holds what. Orthodox Christians also call Mary Theotokos, honor her as ever virgin, and celebrate her falling asleep and her glory. Other Christians hold some of these teachings and not others. This path describes the Catholic teaching, and ranks no one.

segments.voice: On each slow breath, name one of the four and let a picture come with it: Mother of God, a mother holding a child; ever virgin, a closed garden gate; Immaculate Conception, a clean first page; Assumption, someone lifted home. If one puzzles you, let it; questions are welcome. If you pray, greet Mary with Elizabeth's words, the mother of my Lord.
Dogma. A truth the Church teaches as revealed, defined so it can be held with confidence: lights along the path. Four of them concern Mary.

1328.title: Ever virgin (CCC 499–501)
1328.hook: Catholics and Orthodox hold that Mary remained a virgin; some Protestants read the brothers of Jesus differently
1328.howItsDone: Catholics call Mary ever virgin in the liturgy, including in the Confiteor at Mass, and the Orthodox call her ever-virgin in their prayers; the teaching is explained in the Catechism, paragraphs 496 to 501.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dogma: lights along the path, and four of them about Mary. Your line was four teachings.

Jesus comes back to his hometown and teaches in the synagogue, and the town can't get past who he is. Isn't this the carpenter? Isn't his mother called Mary? Then they name names: his brothers, James and Joseph and Simon and Jude, and his sisters too, right here among us. Readers still stop at that line: brothers? Today takes the second of yesterday's four teachings slowly, and that question with it. Today's word: ever virgin.
screen: `ISN'T THIS THE CARPENTER?` → `HIS BROTHERS, HIS SISTERS.` → `EVER VIRGIN.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says Mary's virginity was real and lasting: before Jesus' birth, in it, and for the rest of her life. In the liturgy she's called ever virgin. It starts with her question to the angel, in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" The Church reads her whole life as a yes given entirely to God, and her virginity as a sign of it: a heart, and a body, kept for the one who came to live in it. Then the brothers. The Catechism answers the Nazareth line directly. James and Joseph, two of the names, are called elsewhere in Matthew the sons of another Mary, a disciple of Jesus. The brothers and sisters, it says, are close relations of Jesus, in a way of speaking the Old Testament also uses, where relatives are called brothers. Some early Christian writers thought they were Joseph's children from before he married Mary. Others thought they were cousins. And who reads what. The Catholic and Orthodox churches both teach that Mary remained a virgin; the Orthodox call her ever-virgin in their prayers. Some Protestants read the brothers as later children of Mary and Joseph, and some do not. Each reads the same pages carefully. One more line from the Catechism: Jesus is Mary's only son, but her motherhood reaches out to everyone he came to save. In Catholic teaching, ever virgin doesn't make her distant. It frees her to be mother to many.

1329.title: The new Eve
1329.hook: Irenaeus: the knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience
1329.howItsDone: Catholics meet the new Eve in homilies on Mary, and in the Mass readings for the Immaculate Conception, where Genesis 3 is read alongside Luke 1; the Catechism teaches it at paragraph 494.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ever virgin, and Mary's honest question to the angel: how shall this be done? Your line was ever virgin.

Two women, two conversations, far apart in the Bible. In a garden, a woman listens to the serpent and reaches for the fruit. In a small house in Nazareth, a young woman listens to an angel, and answers: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Early Christian writers set those scenes side by side, like two pages held up to the light. One of them, a bishop named Irenaeus, saw a knot in the first and the same knot coming loose in the second. Today's word: the new Eve.
screen: `A GARDEN AND A SERPENT.` → `A HOUSE AND AN ANGEL.` → `TWO PAGES HELD UP TO THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: You met the new Eve briefly on day three hundred forty; today, the knot. Paul started the pattern. He sets Jesus beside Adam and calls him the last Adam: where the first man brought death, Christ brings life. Irenaeus took it one step further. If there's a new Adam, isn't there a new Eve beside him? Then the knot. Irenaeus wrote that the knot tied by Eve's disobedience was loosened by Mary's obedience, and that what one virgin bound through unbelief, the other set free through faith. The Catechism quotes him, and adds his other line: that Mary, by obeying, became a cause of salvation for herself and for the whole human race. Why a knot? In Irenaeus's picture it isn't cut. It's untied the way it was tied, in reverse. Eve listened to the wrong voice; Mary listens to the right one. Eve doubted the word; Mary trusts it. Eve reached; Mary receives. The second story walks back through the first, undoing it. Then the name. In Genesis, Adam names his wife Eve, in the Douay-Rheims, "because she was the mother of all the living." Christians who call Mary the new Eve hear in her a second mother of the living: mother of the one who is life, and, in Catholic teaching, of everyone who lives in him. None of this makes Mary the savior; the Church is clear that her yes is itself a gift of her son's grace. But it makes her yes enormous.
screen: `A NEW ADAM, A NEW EVE.` · `WHAT ONE BOUND, THE OTHER LOOSED.` · `UNTIED THE WAY IT WAS TIED.` · `MOTHER OF ALL THE LIVING.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Think of one invitation you've been resisting, a call to return, a task you keep postponing, a kindness you know is being asked of you, and notice the knot of reasons and fear tied around it. Without forcing anything, picture what one small yes would look like: not the whole thing, one loosened loop. If you pray, borrow Mary's words: be it done to me according to thy word.
New Eve. Mary, set beside Eve by early Christian writers: where Eve's no tied the knot, Mary's yes untied it.

1330.title: Undoer of knots
1330.hook: a painting in Augsburg shows Mary untying a knotted ribbon, and the devotion travels with Pope Francis
1330.howItsDone: Catholics who keep this devotion pray before copies of the Augsburg image, often with the rosary or a novena, naming a particular trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new Eve: Irenaeus and the knot that Mary's yes untied. Your line was the knot untied.

Above an altar in a church in Augsburg, in Germany, hangs a painting. Mary stands in the middle, with angels around her. On one side, an angel hands her a long white ribbon full of knots, and her hands are busy, working one loose. On the other side, another angel carries the ribbon away, smooth. That's the whole drama: a woman patiently untying knots. Yesterday's line from Irenaeus has a face. Today's word: undoer of knots.
screen: `A PAINTING IN AUGSBURG.` → `A RIBBON FULL OF KNOTS.` → `HANDS AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Tradition links the picture to Irenaeus's knot: what Eve's disobedience tied, Mary's obedience loosened. The canvas gives an ancient bishop's sentence a ribbon and a pair of hands. In the devotion that grew around the painting, the knots are the tangles of a life: a marriage in trouble, a family that won't speak, a habit that won't let go, a fear wound so tight there's no loose end to pull. People bring their own knot to Mary and ask her to pray for them, that with God's grace it may work loose. Then how it traveled. The story goes that a young Jesuit from Argentina, Jorge Mario Bergoglio, came across the image while studying in Germany. Back in Buenos Aires, he gave out cards with the picture, and a devotion took root there. He later became Pope Francis. And the patience in it. Look at Mary's hands. She isn't slashing the ribbon with a knife. A knot pulled hard gets tighter. A knot worked slowly, a little this way and a little that, gives. That's one picture of how grace can work: not all at once, but loop by loop. In Catholic teaching Mary doesn't replace God here. She prays, as a mother would, and God does the untying through her prayer.
screen: `IRENAEUS'S KNOT, PAINTED.` · `THE KNOTS OF A LIFE.` · `FROM GERMANY TO BUENOS AIRES.` · `NOT CUT: WORKED LOOSE.` · then, large: `SHE UNDOES KNOTS.`

segments.voice: Let one knot in your life come to mind, just one, and look at it honestly: where it's tight, and what keeps pulling it tighter. Then imagine handing that stretch of ribbon to someone with patient hands; you don't have to see how it comes undone. If you pray, ask Mary, undoer of knots, to pray for you with the words of the Hail Mary; if you don't, simply loosen your grip a little.
